cards.title: Use Four Funnel Metrics to Locate Where Ad Spend Leaks
cards.summary: Define cost per lead, lead conversion rate, average order value and ROAS, and chain them from spend to revenue so you can see which stage to fix.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a paid campaign or funnel is working and identifying which stage — traffic, opt-in, purchase or upsell — is the bottleneck.

cards.title: Gate a Discount Behind Email Capture at the Buy Moment
cards.summary: Ask for an email in exchange for 5–10% off right before purchase so you can re-contact abandoners and keep marketing after the sale.
cards.use_when: Setting up store acquisition and deciding what a new visitor is asked for first, especially on a PDP or cart entry.

cards.title: Add a Post-Purchase Offer to Raise Average Order Value
cards.summary: Present one complementary item right after the order confirmation, accepting that most buyers decline because the lift from those who don't is the point.
cards.use_when: You sell a product with an obvious companion item and want more revenue per existing buyer without raising ad spend.

cards.title: Point Every Channel at One Shared Front-End Offer
cards.summary: Give paid ads, video and social content the same free-entry destination so channels reinforce each other instead of competing.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative and deciding what the offer, qualifying line and landing target should be across platforms.

cards.title: Choose Where the Next-Tier Offer Appears in the Journey
cards.summary: Decide between an at-checkout upsell, an in-product content promotion, or both in sequence for buyers who decline.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to introduce your next price tier and how to recover buyers who decline the first upsell.

cards.title: Treat Copy as One Layer of a Working Marketing Stack
cards.summary: Copy is the visible layer over email sequences, automations, landing pages, offers and funnels — value comes from building the whole stack, not only the words.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to learn or build next for your store's marketing, and whether copy alone is enough to move revenue.

cards.title: Write a one-paragraph messaging strategy before any copy
cards.summary: A short written messaging strategy gives every copy and design decision a rationale so you stop choosing words by what 'sounds good'.
cards.use_when: You are about to write or rewrite PDP copy, homepage copy or ad creative for a store and need a shared standard for what the copy should do, especially when several people or freelancers touch it.

cards.title: Do customer research before writing a single word of copy
cards.summary: Your store's messages should come from potential customers' language and motivations, not from why you built the product.
cards.use_when: You are preparing PDP copy, ad creative, taglines or a homepage and are tempted to start from internal assumptions about why people buy.

cards.title: Define your primary target segment before writing copy
cards.summary: Pick the segment most likely to visit often and to compensate you in cash or referrals, then write for that segment rather than a generic market.
cards.use_when: You are deciding who your homepage, PDP or ad messages should speak to, or you suspect your copy is trying to please everyone.

cards.title: Run a 12-interview pain-point research round
cards.summary: The source cites Stiehl and DeVries' claim that 12–15 one-on-one interviews surface about 80% of a segment's pain points, matching 7 focus groups.
cards.use_when: You need to identify the pains your product copy and ad hooks should address, and are weighing interviews against focus groups.

cards.title: Separate pain targeting from motivation reflection in copy
cards.summary: Great copy either neutralizes a critical pain or reflects a deep motivation — motivation is not a discount, a limited-time offer or your value proposition.
cards.use_when: You are drafting headline and hero copy for a PDP or landing page and need to decide whether to hit pain or aspiration.

cards.title: Target 20–35% of visitors instead of 100%
cards.summary: Copy written for a narrow, highly qualified segment can convert far better than neutral copy written to offend no one.
cards.use_when: You are writing or revising a homepage headline, PDP headline or ad hook and feel pressure to keep it broad so it does not exclude anyone.

cards.title: Build a product positioning document with five columns
cards.summary: List every feature, mark which are unique, map each to a customer pain and at least one benefit, then priority-rank the rows.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to write PDP copy, comparison content or in-product messaging and need one source of truth about what your product does and why it matters, or you sell multiple products and need one document per product.

cards.title: Distinguish features from benefits and write the customer's outcome
cards.summary: A description of what a feature does is not a benefit; the benefit is the value the specific buyer derives from it.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP bullets or benefit blocks and keep restating specifications instead of outcomes.

cards.title: Choose whether to lead with a benefit or a feature per audience
cards.summary: There is no universal rule that copy must lead with the benefit — some shoppers distrust soft benefit language and go straight to comparison charts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what goes in the hero headline and first bullets of a PDP or landing page for a specific shopper type.

cards.title: Show don't tell: let design and visuals carry part of the message
cards.summary: Some of the strongest messages never appear as text — screenshots and visual design can prove a claim better than copy.
cards.use_when: You are building a PDP, How It Works page or feature section and deciding what to write versus what to show.

cards.title: Audit competitor and search language to skip wordsmithing
cards.summary: Messaging built from exact customer keywords, review phrases and competitor audits removes guesswork from value proposition writing.
cards.use_when: You need headline and value-proposition language for a PDP or ad set and are deciding between internal wording and market wording.

cards.title: Plan messaging for launch traffic waves
cards.summary: Startup traffic arrives in distinct waves with different motivations, and copy may need lines specifically written to reflect each wave's motivation.
cards.use_when: You are sequencing store launch content, early landing pages or ad campaigns and deciding which message to show as traffic sources shift.

cards.title: Test names and creative with cheap ad or shelf experiments
cards.summary: Tim Ferriss' low-budget testing approach — PPC-tested book titles and store-shelf cover tests — transfers to naming products and choosing creative.
cards.use_when: You are choosing a product name, collection name or ad creative set and want market evidence instead of internal preference.

cards.title: Fix headlines that target no one
cards.summary: Copy that could belong to any company in the category signals you are not targeting a segment — make headlines specific.
cards.use_when: You are auditing an existing homepage or PDP headline and it reads generic or interchangeable with competitors.

cards.title: Decide whether to write copy in positive or negative framing
cards.summary: Marketing messages typically stem from solving pain, which is inherently negative, while marketing managers push for positive framing — the source flags this tension.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP or ad copy about a problem the product solves and are choosing between pain-first and positive-outcome-first framing.

cards.title: Run a research survey and select your target segments
cards.summary: Survey at least 12 people, look for surprising and repeated answers rather than validation, then shortlist segments by visit frequency and compensation.
cards.use_when: You are starting from limited customer knowledge and need to pick which segment your store copy and ads should speak to.

cards.title: Show Don't Tell: Convey Benefits Through Design and UI
cards.summary: Your product's interface or page design can demonstrate a core benefit without a single word of copy.
cards.use_when: Designing a PDP, landing page or app onboarding where a core benefit (simplicity, speed, cleanliness) can be demonstrated visually instead of claimed in text.

cards.title: Build a Product Positioning Document Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: A structured table matching unique features to customer pains, benefits and priority ranking is the foundation for all page copy.
cards.use_when: Starting copy for a new product page, landing page or ad campaign and needing a documented, ranked source of messages before writing.

cards.title: Choose Positive vs Negative Framing Based on What's Working
cards.summary: Neither positive nor negative framing wins universally; test both, but never attach your brand to a negative image you can't decisively remove.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to frame a headline, ad hook or landing page message around a customer pain versus a desired outcome.

cards.title: Use Keyword Research to Source Customer Language for Copy
cards.summary: AdWords search volume reveals the exact phrases customers use, which belong in your headlines, buttons and demos — not just your SEO tags.
cards.use_when: Writing headlines, subheads, meta titles, demo scripts or button copy for a product or category page and needing the customer's own vocabulary.

cards.title: Run a Home-Page-Only Competitor Content Audit
cards.summary: Audit up to 10 competitors' home pages for value props, top messages, CTAs, guarantees and standout ideas to inform your own messaging strategy.
cards.use_when: Planning a new home page, category page or landing page and needing to know what messages prospects have already seen from competitors.

cards.title: Build a Messaging Hierarchy Tied to Where Users Look
cards.summary: Rank messages most-to-least important for your target visitor, then place each where users actually look rather than in priority order down the page.
cards.use_when: Laying out a landing page, home page or PDP and deciding which message goes above the fold, near buttons, or further down.

cards.title: Simplify Ambiguous Offers Into One Concrete Statement
cards.summary: Simplify a fee or offer message to a single unambiguous condition; the source's Fidelity example quadrupled program customers in 4 months.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising an offer headline, promo banner, pricing page or loyalty/checkout message that currently contains vague terms.

cards.title: Write Unbelievable-but-True Copy and Back It With Credibility
cards.summary: A nearly-unbelievable line can outperform, but it must never be literally impossible and must be supported by clear examples on the page.
cards.use_when: Drafting a bold claim or hook for a PDP, landing page or ad where the benefit sounds too good to be ordinary.

cards.title: Leverage Related News for a Time-Sensitive Landing Page
cards.summary: When a competitor blunder or relevant news item breaks, build a long-form page around it to redirect demand while the motivation is fresh.
cards.use_when: An industry news event or competitor failure creates momentary interest your store can respond to with a landing page or campaign.

cards.title: Overwrite, Then Cut Vigorously — Long Copy Works If Interesting
cards.summary: Write roughly 10x more than you need, then trim hard; fact-packed long copy outperforms dull short copy.
cards.use_when: Drafting a long-form landing page, sales page or product story and deciding how much to write and how hard to edit.

cards.title: Don't Over-Explain; Assume Less Analytical Readers
cards.summary: Readers aren't constantly scrutinizing every claim, so you don't need to justify each statement — but don't exploit their blind acceptance either.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much explanation and justification to include in page copy, descriptions or ad text without bloating it.

cards.title: Treat Positioning as the Highest-Leverage Copy Decision
cards.summary: The source calls positioning the most important decision; decide it through research before writing a single word.
cards.use_when: Before writing any product page, category page or ad campaign — when deciding what your product fundamentally is in the customer's mind.

cards.title: Write Ads to Trigger the Life-Force 8 Biological Desires
cards.summary: Anchor product messaging to one of eight hardwired human desires that drive the majority of purchasing decisions.
cards.use_when: Choosing the core angle for a PDP headline, ad creative or launch campaign when deciding which emotional benefit to lead with.

cards.title: Direct Mental Movies With Specific Visual Words
cards.summary: Replace vague benefit claims with specific visual language that makes prospects mentally simulate using the product.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, ad body copy, landing page sections or video scripts where a generic benefit statement is falling flat.

cards.title: Lead With 'What's In It For Me?' Benefits
cards.summary: Consumers care about what the product does for them, not company facts, equipment or process.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product pages, about sections, ad copy or brochures that currently describe the company, factory or product specs.

cards.title: Build Fear Appeals With All Four Required Components
cards.summary: Fear only converts when it is strong, paired with a specific effective solution, and the prospect believes they can act.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy or a landing page for a protective or problem-solving product (security, insurance, hygiene, safety gear, health supplements).

cards.title: Use Ego Morphing to Sell Identity, Not Just Function
cards.summary: Present imagery and social proof that lets buyers see themselves as the kind of person who owns the product.
cards.use_when: Merchandising lifestyle, luxury, apparel, beauty or status-adjacent products where functional copy underperforms.

cards.title: Pair the Scare With a Credible, Easy Solution
cards.summary: Fear appeals must translate into a believable, achievable action or they create inaction.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative for problem-solution products like sanitizers, supplements, insurance or safety items.

cards.title: Use Psychologically Potent Headlines to Stop the Scroll
cards.summary: The headline is the highest-leverage copy element; use proven starters and lead with the strongest benefit.
cards.use_when: Running paid social or display ads, writing email subject lines, or title-tagging a PDP or landing page.

cards.title: Battle Human Inertia at the Point of Decision
cards.summary: Even a convinced buyer needs reasons to act now and an easy path to purchase.
cards.use_when: Optimizing checkout, cart recovery, subscription sign-up or any step where visitors have interest but don't convert.

cards.title: Borrow Credibility Through Social Proof and Authority
cards.summary: Prospects need to believe your claims before they buy; transfer credibility via testimonials, transfer and authority positioning.
cards.use_when: Adding trust elements to a PDP, landing page, sales letter or paid ad for a product with a skeptical or high-consideration audience.

cards.title: Structure Copy for Clarity and Reinforce Key Points
cards.summary: Message clarity and repetition are separate, stackable persuasive techniques.
cards.use_when: Editing long-form sales pages, email sequences, or any asset that feels scattered or unclear after the first draft.

cards.title: Match Copy to the Buyer's Stage and End Goal
cards.summary: Persuasion step-by-step (Transtheoretical Model) and means-end chaining help you align message with where the buyer is and what they're really after.
cards.use_when: Planning email sequences, retargeting ads or content marketing where different segments need different messages.

cards.title: Apply Layout, Type and Color to Increase Readership
cards.summary: Formatting choices affect how many people actually read and act on your ad.
cards.use_when: Laying out a PDP, landing page, email or ad creative where copy is already strong but engagement is low.

cards.title: Use Specificity and the Ogilvy Principle to Stand Out
cards.summary: Extreme specificity and following Ogilvy's evidence-based principles set your copy apart from vague competitor claims.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing any claim in a product description, ad or landing page that currently reads generically.

cards.title: Test Offers Like a Direct-Response Marketer
cards.summary: Treat the offer, not the copy alone, as the primary testable variable.
cards.use_when: Structuring an A/B testing roadmap for an ecommerce store's landing pages, PDPs or email campaigns.

cards.title: Prioritize Metrics That Reflect Action, Not Applause
cards.summary: Advertising's purpose is to make people act; measure purchases, not entertainment value.
cards.use_when: Setting up dashboards, reviewing a campaign's results, or justifying budget for a direct-response creative project.

cards.title: Use the 46-Point Killer Ad Checklist to Review Assets
cards.summary: A pre-launch checklist catches weak headlines, missing benefits, unclear offers and friction before spend.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a landing page, PDP, paid ad or email before it goes live.

cards.title: Close With a Restated Offer (The P.S. Principle)
cards.summary: The P.S. is often read first; use it to restate the offer and push action.
cards.use_when: Writing sales emails, sales pages or direct-mail-style landing page copy.

cards.title: Ego Appeal Through Envious Comparison
cards.summary: Show the buyer's peers envying them to trigger ego-driven purchase desire for premium products.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative or PDP imagery for a premium, status-signalling product where the buyer's self-image drives the purchase.

cards.title: Transfer: Borrow Credibility From Respected Symbols
cards.summary: Use trusted institutional symbols, seals and expert cues so buyers question your sales argument less.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, landing pages or ad creative for products where prospect skepticism — not awareness — is the main conversion blocker.

cards.title: Bandwagon Effect: Link Products to Reference Groups
cards.summary: Persuade buyers by tying your product to aspirational, associative or dissociative reference groups they identify with.
cards.use_when: Choosing models, testimonials or lifestyle imagery for acquisition creative and brand positioning.

cards.title: Means-End Chain: Sell the Benefit of the Benefit
cards.summary: Write copy and imagery that points to the ultimate end result, so buyers evaluate the outcome instead of scrutinizing the product.
cards.use_when: Drafting PDP copy, hero headlines or ad hooks when the product's raw features are unremarkable or commodity-like.

cards.title: Match Ad Content to Buyer Stage (Transtheoretical Model)
cards.summary: Identify whether prospects are unaware, considering, planning, buying or habitual, then write copy for that stage.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign series, email flow or landing page for a product with varying buyer awareness.

cards.title: Inoculation Theory: Pre-empt Competitors' Attacks
cards.summary: Warn prospects about competitors' claims and weak arguments in advance so they compare purchases through your filter.
cards.use_when: Writing comparison content, objection-handling copy or competitor-differentiation sections on PDPs and landing pages.

cards.title: Belief Re-ranking: Change Beliefs Without Triggering Defensiveness
cards.summary: Change importance of beliefs or offer alternative evidence rather than telling buyers they're wrong.
cards.use_when: Writing copy to shift buyers off a habit or incumbent brand onto your product without triggering reactance.

cards.title: Elaboration Likelihood Model: Choose Central or Peripheral Copy
cards.summary: Match ad content to the buyer's thinking depth — heavy facts for high-consideration purchases, image and cues for low-stakes ones.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much evidence and data versus imagery and celebrity cues to put into a PDP, ad or landing page.

cards.title: Cialdini's Six Cues (CLARCCS) for Peripheral-Route Ads
cards.summary: Deploy comparison, liking, authority, reciprocation, commitment/consistency and scarcity as mental shortcuts in low-consideration ad copy.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative or PDP persuasion blocks for low-cost or impulse purchases where buyers won't deliberate deeply.

cards.title: Reciprocation Offers That Kickstart Purchase
cards.summary: Give genuine value up front to create obligation and start the reciprocation loop toward a paid purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing first-order incentives, new-mover or new-customer offers, samples or lead magnets.

cards.title: Prime Reciprocation with a Genuine Gift (Not a Trinket)
cards.summary: Give prospects a valuable, unrequested gift to trigger the pull of reciprocation and start new-customer relationships.
cards.use_when: Designing a new-customer acquisition offer, welcome insert, or sampling campaign for a store.

cards.title: Commitment/Consistency and the Four-Walls Ad Structure
cards.summary: Build ads that pose a ladder of questions your prospect answers 'yes' to, boxing them into consistency with a stance they've already taken.
cards.use_when: Writing long-form sales copy, landing pages, or email sequences where you want to build momentum toward a purchase.

cards.title: Use Scarcity and Exclusivity to Increase Desire
cards.summary: Frame offers as limited in supply and access so the product appears both scarce and exclusive, raising consumer interest.
cards.use_when: Positioning a launch, sale, drop, or limited-quantity offer on a PDP, landing page, or campaign.

cards.title: Message Organization: Clarity Before Persuasion
cards.summary: If the prospect doesn't understand your message, no amount of testimonials or polish will persuade them - structure and simplify first.
cards.use_when: Reviewing PDP copy, ad copy, or any customer-facing message that feels crowded or confusing before sending it live.

cards.title: Examples Beat Statistics: Trigger Self-Demonstration
cards.summary: Vivid examples make prospects imagine themselves using the product, which drives desire and purchase more than raw specifications.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, PDP hero copy, and ad creatives for any product where emotion drives the purchase.

cards.title: Two-Sided Messages: Compliment the Competition, Then Win
cards.summary: Present your competitor's strengths fairly, then show why you're better - this reads as credible and persuasive.
cards.use_when: Writing comparison pages, PDPs, or ads in a category with a well-known incumbent or a superior alternative that customers will discover anyway.

cards.title: The Takeaway Play: Tell Prospects Why Not to Buy
cards.summary: Telling people why they shouldn't buy can boost credibility and intensify desire among true prospects.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, sales pages, or email for products where some buyers are a poor fit or where the offer risks seeming too good to be true.

cards.title: Repetition vs. Redundancy: Extend an Ad's Life Without Burning It Out
cards.summary: Repetition builds familiarity and trust, but overuse breeds contempt; re-present the same message in different formats to reset attention.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign flighting for a proven ad or a product's ongoing promotions.

cards.title: Rhetorical Questions: Use for Retention, Not Assumed Persuasion
cards.summary: Rhetorical questions may boost message retention and attention but the evidence on persuasion is mixed.
cards.use_when: Choosing headline or hook formats for ads, email subject lines, or PDP hero copy where you need attention or memory.

cards.title: WIIFM: Customers Buy Only When Believed Value Exceeds the Price
cards.summary: Prospects must first understand what's in it for them; without that, they won't even consider the trade.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your PDP or offer page to check whether the benefit to the buyer is front and center.

cards.title: Use Verifiable Evidence to Convert Belief into Purchase
cards.summary: Evidence - facts, figures, testimonials, endorsements, research, charts - persuades more effectively than claims you made yourself.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for higher-priced or considered-purchase products where prospects need justification before buying.

cards.title: Length-Implies-Strength: Let Volume and Numbers Signal Credibility
cards.summary: Long, fact-packed copy and large numbers of testimonials or reasons make prospects infer the product must be legitimate.
cards.use_when: Writing sales pages, testimonials pages, or proof-heavy PDP sections for products where credibility is the main obstacle.

cards.title: Heuristics: Leverage Lazy-Brain Shortcuts in Ad Design
cards.summary: Because most buyers prefer fast, low-effort decisions, structure ads to deliver information in short, intuitive cues.
cards.use_when: Designing overall ad layouts, PDP structures, and proof blocks where customers are likely to skim.

cards.title: The Psychology of Simplicity: Readable Copy Is Non-Negotiable
cards.summary: Advertising exists to get people to act, so it must be written to be understood - simple, direct, and readable.
cards.use_when: Final QA on ad copy, PDP text, email, and any customer-facing copy before it ships.

cards.title: Score Copy with the Flesch Reading Ease Formula
cards.summary: Use the Flesch Reading Ease Score in your writing tool to enforce readable copy across ads and pages.
cards.use_when: Editing product pages, ads, and email drafts for readability before publishing.

cards.title: Vary Your Tools but Keep a Readability Floor on Ad Copy
cards.summary: Ad copy that scores at postgraduate reading level loses mass audiences; keep the readability low enough for broad consumption.
cards.use_when: Deciding how technical or formal your product copy should be on a PDP or ad creative.

cards.title: Rewrite Vague Claims with Short Words and Concrete Promises
cards.summary: Trade formal abstraction for specific, benefit-led phrasing that the reader can see and believe.
cards.use_when: Editing benefit claims, headlines, and PDP bullets to make them more concrete and persuasive.

cards.title: Run the Same Message Through Multiple Sources and Arguments
cards.summary: Present the same claim from several different people and lightly varied arguments to shift belief.
cards.use_when: Building testimonial blocks, review sections, creator partnerships, and multi-channel campaigns for one product.

cards.title: Plain-Language Rewrite of Product Copy
cards.summary: Strip school-taught 'big words' from product descriptions and ad copy so shoppers instantly understand what you sell.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a product page, category description, paid-ad copy or email when traffic bounces or copy reads like a corporate brochure.
